agree.reason: The frank admission that the firm is going back on its word and the clear no-exceptions line will earn respect, but the remote hires far from the office get only a $150 subsidy and a four-month delay, so the ones who stay mainly for remote work have little reason not to leave.

honest.reason: The dates and figures match the brief, but 'we're seeing the same problem inside the firm', 'capable of doing' and the claim that people learn to lead by sitting next to leaders go beyond what the brief says and present a causal link as settled.

works_the_facts.reason: The facts are mostly restated rather than worked: the draft never says that 15 of 46 is about a third, never uses the 5-of-6 project leads as a measure of what already works, and puts the far-away concession in its least favourable form ('only four months longer').

right_comparison.reason: It never describes what happens if remote work continues, such as more lost interviews or continued slow progression for juniors, so readers have no picture of the alternative to compare against.

qualification.reason: The six-month review is the only condition, and it gives no measure, no threshold and no consequence, so readers cannot tell what might change the policy or check whether it worked.

objections.reason: It deals head-on with the broken hiring promise, desk shortages and hopes of exceptions, and the partners' own commitment answers the fairness complaint, but it leaves out the obvious objections: why three days rather than fewer, and whether remote work is really what slows junior progression.

fit.reason: It is a one-page email with a clear subject line and short headed sections, and it ends by pointing to the Friday meeting, which is exactly the format the brief asked for.
